title: Auth middleware
idea: `requireAuth` is a middleware that guards a route. It verifies the bearer token, stores the caller on `req.user`, and calls `next()`.
points: `requireAuth` reads `req.get('authorization')` and expects two words: `Bearer` and the token.
`verifyToken` throws on a bad signature or an expired token. The middleware catches it.
On success `req.user` is `{ id, email }`. The id is `Number(claims.sub)`, matching `users.id`.
Every failure, whatever the cause, answers `401` with `{ error: 'Unauthorized' }`.

messages.label: GET + Bearer token
messages.note: The client sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. `requireAuth` splits it at the space.

messages.label: verifyToken(token)
messages.note: The scheme is `Bearer` and a token is present, so `requireAuth` hands the token to the helper.

messages.label: claims
messages.note: The signature and expiry check out. The helper returns `sub`, `email` and the timestamps.

messages.label: next()
messages.note: `requireAuth` sets `req.user` to `{ id, email }`, then calls `next()`.

messages.label: 200 + data
messages.note: The handler reads `req.user`. It never parses a header itself.

messages.label: GET, no header
messages.note: A second request has no `Authorization` header.

messages.label: 401 Unauthorized
messages.note: `requireAuth` answers at once. `verifyToken` and the handler never run.

messages.label: GET + bad token
messages.note: A third request carries a tampered or expired token.

messages.label: verifyToken(token)
messages.note: The scheme looks right, so `requireAuth` asks the helper.

messages.label: throws
messages.note: The helper throws. `requireAuth` catches it and sends `401`. The handler does not run.

code.title: requireAuth
code.caption: The middleware is the new code. The rest copies lecture 11's helpers and adds a stand-in route.

walk.text: A short copy of lecture 11's helpers, so this file runs alone.
Split the header at the space. Anything but `Bearer <token>` gets the one shared `401` reply.
`verifyToken` throws on a bad or expired token. Catch it and send `401`.
Store the caller on `req.user`, then call `next()`. Only now does the route run.
A stand-in route that returns `req.user` and counts how often it runs.
Four requests: no header, a valid token, the wrong scheme and an expired token.
Only the valid request reaches the handler. The counter shows it ran once.

pitfalls: Return after sending `401`. Otherwise the function carries on and calls `next()` too.
`requireAuth` never queries the database. A deleted user's token works until it expires.
Take the user from `req.user`, never from the body or query string.

quiz.why: A valid token calls `next()`. Junk makes `verifyToken` throw, and a missing header fails the `Bearer` check. Both send `401`.

takeaway: Verify the token once, in middleware; handlers then trust `req.user`.

starters: Why catch the error instead of letting Express handle it?
Should `requireAuth` load the user from the database?
How do I protect only some routes and leave `GET /:shortCode` public?
